title: Accepting the will
hookLine: bhaana is sweet acceptance of what the Lord sends

lines: YOUR DOING SEEMS SWEET TO ME.
cards: Tera keeya meetha laagai. A short line from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raag Asa: your doing seems sweet to me. Sikhs sing it in kirtan, and it's easy to hum without hearing how bold it is.
It doesn't say your doing is easy, or what I wanted. It says sweet. About whatever comes.
Tradition ties the line to Guru Arjan's own last days, which were anything but sweet. Today's word is the inner turn that makes a line like that possible: bhaana.

teach.b: First, the word. Bhaana is the will of the Lord, what pleases the Lord, the way things come to us; you met it early on this path, in an Ardas said in grief. Sikhs speak of bhaana mannana: accepting the will.
It sits close to Hukam. Hukam is the order itself; bhaana is that order arriving in your own life, on an ordinary day, as news you didn't ask for. Second, the line in full.

teach.h: NOT A NEW OUTCOME, BUT THE NAME.
teach.b: In paraphrase: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak asks for the treasure of the Lord's Name. Not a different outcome. The Name.
The prayer turns from changing what happened to staying close to the One it came from. Third, the hardest part.
Tradition says Guru Arjan was tortured in Lahore and died there, and that through it he kept repeating this very line.
Sikhs remember that as bhaana at its hardest: not a calm man in a calm room, but a man in agony, still saying sweet. Fourth, what bhaana is not. It isn't giving up.
The same tradition tells how his son, the Sixth Guru, took up arms. Sikhs feed the hungry, stand against injustice, go to the doctor, fix what can be fixed.
Bhaana is the heart's stance toward what has already come, not an excuse to stop acting on what can still change.
It's taking what arrived, even bitter, and refusing to let it push the Lord out of the room.

how: Sikhs speak of bhaana mannana, accepting the Lord's will, especially in loss; the shabad tera keeya meetha laagai is often sung in kirtan, and Sikhs recall it in connection with Guru Arjan's martyrdom.

o: a prayer asking God to undo what happened
fate that can't be changed, so effort is pointless
the Lord's will, as it arrives in your own life

games.q: what's inside bhaana: tap the pairs.
p: the will, arriving in a life
your doing seems sweet to me

s: accepting the will means giving up and doing nothing
Sikhs still feed the hungry and stand against injustice; bhaana is the heart's stance toward what has already come.
the line 'your doing seems sweet to me' is by Guru Arjan
it's in a hymn in Raag Asa, and tradition ties it to his last days.
in the hymn, Nanak asks for the bad thing to be taken away
he asks for the treasure of the Lord's Name.

games.q: something you can't change has just gone wrong. the Guru's line is in your head. which response matches bhaana?
o: accept what came, and still do what can be done.
games.why: bhaana accepts what has come without becoming a shrug; the same tradition tells of the Sixth Guru taking up arms.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've been resisting that you truly cannot change: not an injustice you could act on, but something that has simply happened, a delay, a no, a body slower than it was.

On the in-breath, name it; on the out-breath, try the word accepted, and see if any part of you can loosen. Sweet may be too far today; lighter is enough, and if you pray, you can hum the Guru's line.

wordCard.voice: Bhaana. The will of the Lord, as it arrives in a life; bhaana mannana is accepting it, sweetly, while still doing what can be done. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the will, what pleases the Lord; bhaana mannana is to accept it.

carryVoice: Your line: his will. Not a shrug: acceptance, with hands still working. See you on the path tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 394 (Asa, Guru Arjan: tera keeya meetha laagai, har naam padaarath naanak maangai)
